This is based on misconceptions and misinformation.

I play Doom classic in VR on a pretty regular basis and am perfectly fine. Most people are. Doom was one of the earliest things to get converted into VR thanks to ZDoom.

First of all, it's VR sickness not motion sickness. They're actually exact opposites and have similar symptoms, but are not the same thing. One is caused by the body feeling motion when a person is stationary and the brain not agreeing with it, and the other is caused by the brain perceiving motion when the body isn't feeling it. They are literally caused by reversed sensations.

Secondly, it's actually pretty rare for someone to actually get VR sickness in properly done VR. If you've got low latency and a high enough framerate, it's pretty comfortable even in motion for the vast majority of people. Only a very small portion of people actually get sick, and even then it's a build up and doesn't happen instantly.

The vast majority of people are perfectly fine with gamepad motion in VR. It's just a handful of outliers that have problems.

Sure, that does need to be addressed, but this thing where people are constantly told 'you'll get sick' is false. Most people won't be bothered in the slightest.

I've demoed VR for a lot of people, and basically no one got sick or even dizzy with gamepad based controls with normal movement in Doom. In fact, movement much worse than Doom has proven comfortable for most. Windlands has you swinging around an environment like Spider-Man and I've yet to encounter anyone who became ill playing it. I also do Minecraft with standard controls and am fine, most people are. Same goes for Sublevel Zero, Elite Dangerous, the Star Wars X-wing demo I've got, and lots of other games and demos that utilize standard controls and movement.

VR that runs as it should is comfortable for the vast majority of people even with twitch based games like shooters and unusual movement. It's just a small minority that have troubles with it, and even then most of those people will adjust if they take it slow and gain 'VR legs' by gradual exposure.

Also, the thing with HUDs depends on the person, and again is pretty rare. In fact, having a static element actually helps a lot of people adapt to VR. This is why some people who have difficulty with standard motion are fine in driving/flying simulators. The cockpit view helps the brain adapt for a lot of people.

Overall you're making a pretty uncommon problem sound like it's a lot more common than it actually is.

I'd even argue that a lot of the cases of people getting sick in VR are because of substandard hardware that is struggling with framerates. People trying to do too more than their system can handle and ending up with a sub-par experience as a result with latency and a framerate that's too low.

There's no reason most can't play things like Skyrim or WoW in VR today provided they have the hardware to run it properly. In fact, Skyrim is another thing I've done, have demoed for others, and everyone has been perfectly fine.

I'd suggest trying VR out and seeing how it works for you before investing in it if possible. Even if it gives you a little trouble, be aware that most people can adapt to it over time with gradual exposure.

Telling people they shouldn't bother trying to play something or that they don't want games in VR based on a rare outlying issue that most people don't have is bad advice. Even if it doesn't feel great after a short while at first, VR is something you can build up a tolerance for.

I don't have a problem with new control systems that can help players with issues adapt, but they also shouldn't ruin everyone else's fun, become forced features, or stifle development based on a small minority.

It's like saying people shouldn't be able to use sailboats because a some people get seasick. That sucks for those people and there are ways to mitigate it, but if everyone else is fine there's no reason to put everyone else out over it and not offer standard movement as an option for those who can handle it.

Teleport movement is not a cure all. It's a nice feature that can help some people adapt to VR gaming, but that doesn't mean that it should be -the- standard either considering most people are fine without it.

I don't see any reason to tell people not to bother with standard movement just because there's a small chance that it might make them feel a bit off. Chances are it won't, and even if it does it's not an immediate effect. You can feel it coming on and stop before it sets in.

I've gotten that off feeling from bad VR myself when I tried to run demanding games at settings that were too high for my hardware to run in VR properly. Dialing things back and hitting a high enough framerate over having everything look amazing solved the problem. Having everything look its absolute best is nice, but it'll have to wait for a hardware upgrade for some games.

You're vastly overstating a problem only a small minority suffer from.

Doom will not 'wreck' most people in VR, nor does that type of movement for most people. Same goes for HUDs. Most people are fine with them. Having them off the display is better for immersion, but I don't believe for a moment that they contribute to VR sickness outside of maybe the placebo effect.

If that was really the actual cause of the problem then HUD displays on visors and lenses in real life would make people sick, and they don't.

Rather than avoiding playing games normally, maybe you should try gradually adapting yourself to them? Being able to use standard controls to move helps with immersion a lot in larger environments. Being stuck in a room sized space kind of defeats the point of VR, and teleporting around isn't the same. I've tried both and was unimpressed, standard movement just feels better if you can handle it.

Sorry if you can't, but like I said, it's something that even most people who have issues can adjust to over time. Especially if they don't try to take it too fast and work at it gradually. Most people won't even need to and will be perfectly fine with standard movement.

TL;DR

Dude mistakenly believes that because he gets sick in VR, that most other people do as well. Most people don't and are perfectly fine with standard controls and movement. People that get sick from properly done VR with standard movement controls are a minority, not the majority.

As his advice does not pertain to most people, it's not very good. Especially considering that even people who get sick from VR can gain what is known as 'VR Legs' with gradual exposure over a period of time and get used to VR so it doesn't make them sick anymore.

Also, VR sickness and Motion Sickness are not the same thing. They are somewhat similar, but caused by exact opposite sensations on the brain and body. The two are literally the reverse of each other, and while share some similar symptoms, don't actually affect people in quite the same way.
